source.title: A Comparison of Single Leg Countermovement Jump Techniques on Jump Performance: Considerations for Test Standardization

paper.citation: Staton AE, Fahey J, Jones PA. A comparison of single leg countermovement jump techniques on jump performance: considerations for test standardization. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2026.
paper.abstract: This within-subject study compared four single leg countermovement jump (SLCMJ) techniques in 24 university sports science students to improve test standardization for sport and rehabilitation testing. Reliability and performance were assessed across outcome, kinetic, temporal and kinematic metrics in a single session. The free-limb technique (D) was hypothesised to give greater outcome values because of greater free-limb action.
paper.tldr: Jump height reliability was acceptable for all four SLCMJ techniques, but the technique used changed jump height, timing and force values, so one technique should be fixed and recorded. In this sample the 90 degree knee bend (B) was the most reliable across most metrics, although the results come from non-elite students tested in one session.
paper.methods: Twenty-four university students (19 male, 5 female; mean age 21.4 years, SD 3.7) completed three trials of each of four techniques on both limbs in randomized order within one session. Vertical ground reaction force came from a single Hawkin Dynamics force plate at 1000 Hz, with 2D video at 100 fps for kinematics. Relative reliability used ICC(1,3) and absolute reliability used the coefficient of variation, and between-technique differences used repeated-measures ANOVA or the Friedman test, with Bonferroni-corrected post hoc tests.
paper.findings: System weight was reliable for every technique (ICC 1.00), and jump height reliability was acceptable for all techniques (ICC 0.88 to 0.96, CV 7.05 to 9.81%), while take-off kinematic reliability was unacceptable for all techniques (ICC at or below 0.70). Technique B (90 degree knee bend) had the highest reliability across most metrics, although its values do not fully support the abstract's summary of an ICC of at least 0.80 and a CV of at most 13%. Technique D had greater jump height than A, B and C on both limbs, with greater jump momentum than A and C on the left and than A, B and C on the right; technique C had shorter time to take-off than B and D on both limbs; and mRSI did not differ significantly between techniques on either limb.
paper.limitations: The sample was mostly amateur, included only 5 women with no sex-specific results, tested no injured athletes, and used one session, so between-session reliability and the rehabilitation use the authors discuss are untested. The authors say the mechanism behind technique D needs 3D motion analysis, and only one force plate and one video set-up were used. Check these points in the source PDF before quoting them: the SD of 0.64 for technique D left countermovement depth looks like a print error, the technique A left-limb jump height ICC of 0.88 has a confidence interval (0.91 to 0.96) that does not contain it, and the abstract says dual force plates while the Methods describe a single one.
paper.practicalImplications: Because jump height, time to take-off and jump momentum changed with technique, a practitioner who compares tests over time or between limbs should fix one SLCMJ technique and record which one was used. Technique D gave greater jump heights through a different movement strategy that the authors say still needs 3D confirmation, so it is the less standardised choice.
paper.athleteDev: Jump height was acceptable for monitoring with every technique in this sample, whereas take-off kinematics were unreliable and time to take-off was poor for technique D. Practitioners should treat those timing and kinematic measures with caution when tracking athletes.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-play decisions. It tested no injured athletes, so the rehabilitation use the authors discuss is untested, and its reliability values come from uninjured amateur students tested in one session.
